title: Can buyers bring buyers?
principle: A loop where buyers bring buyers beats paying for each one.

screens.text: Let me tell you about Hotmail. In July 1996, Sabeer Bhatia, who grew up in India, and Jack Smith started a free email service on the web. They did not spend on big ads. Instead, every email had a short line at the bottom: "Get your free email at Hotmail."

screens.prompt: Every email a user sent carried that line. What do you think happened next?

options.label: It grew slowly with small ads
People complained and the line was removed
A million people joined within six months

screens.why: A million people joined within six months. Each email carried a small ad to a friend, who could also join for free. Then that friend's emails reached more people. In December 1997, Microsoft bought Hotmail.

screens.title: Growth loops
screens.text: This is a growth loop. Each buyer helps bring another buyer. When you stop paying for ads, they stop bringing people. But a loop can keep working. We measure it with the K-factor: new buyers per buyer. If 10 buyers bring 5 more, K is 0.5.

screens.prompt: In April, 20 families order cakes. Their party guests bring 6 new families in May. What is your K-factor?
screens.why: Right. 6 new families ÷ 20 buyers = 0.3. Each buyer brings 0.3 new buyers on average. But when K is below 1, the loop cannot grow by itself. You still need other ways to find buyers.

wrong.b: You divided 20 by 6. Do it the other way: new families ÷ buyers. So 6 ÷ 20 = 0.3.
wrong.c: 6 is the number of new families. K-factor means new families per buyer. So 6 ÷ 20 = 0.3.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Every Hotmail email showed its name. Your cakes also reach new people at parties. It's late May. About 15 guests see each birthday cake. Some ask the family, "Who made this?" But most families forget your name or number.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six ideas. For each one, tell me: does it help buyers bring more buyers, or do you pay to reach people?

items.text: A small card with your number in every cake box
An Instagram post you pay to show to more people
A thank-you note in each box asking buyers to share your number
Pay ₹2,000 to a food blogger for one post
Your WhatsApp number printed on the cake board
Flyers handed out at the market

screens.why: Good. A loop uses something your buyer already does, like opening a cake box or sharing cake with guests. Paid ads bring new people only while you pay.

screens.prompt: True or false: once you have a growth loop, you never need to spend money to find customers.

options.label: True: the loop brings all new buyers
False: you still need other ways

screens.why: False. When K-factor is below 1, each group of buyers brings fewer new buyers than the last. So the loop gets smaller unless you keep finding buyers in other ways.

wrong.a: Only when K stays above 1 can the loop grow by itself. With K at 0.3, 20 families bring 6. Those 6 bring about 2. So you still need other ways to find buyers.

screens.prompt: A happy family says, "We'll tell all our friends about you!" How will you check if your growth loop works?

options.label: Believe the family will tell their friends
Ask how many friends they told about you
Count how many friends placed an order

screens.why: Right. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. Ask every new buyer, "How did you hear about us?" Then count how many came from other buyers. This helps you find your K-factor.

wrong.a: Happy words are good to hear, but they are not proof. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. Count the orders that came from friends.
wrong.b: Saying "We told ten friends" does not mean those friends ordered. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. Count orders from friends.

screens.setup: It's the end of May. Cards in cake boxes now bring 6 new families for every 20 orders. You have ₹4,000 to spend on finding more buyers. Each cake leaves you ₹450. Count only the first cake each family buys.
screens.question: How will you spend the ₹4,000?

options.label: Spend all ₹4,000 on Instagram video ads
options.outcome: The ads bring 10 families. Their first cakes leave you ₹4,500. After paying ₹4,000, you have ₹500 left. When you stop the ads, they stop bringing new families.
options.why: Ads can bring in more money than they cost. You'll check that sum soon. But here, you paid to get each buyer. When the ads ended, they stopped bringing new families.
options.better: Give ₹50 off to the family and ₹50 off to each friend who orders. This encourages buyers to bring friends.

options.label: Give ₹50 off to families and their friends
options.outcome: Families start sharing your number. Now 20 orders bring 12 new families instead of 6. The 6 extra families leave you ₹2,700. The ₹50 discounts cost ₹1,200. So you have ₹1,500 more. The new families also start bringing friends.
options.why: You gave families a reason to share your number. Your K-factor doubled from 0.3 to 0.6. The loop can keep bringing new buyers next month.

options.label: Spend ₹4,000 on boxes with your name
options.outcome: The boxes cost ₹4,000. Guests like them, but few ask for your number. Now 20 orders bring 7 new families, just 1 more than before. You spent ₹4,000 to earn only ₹450 more. So you lost ₹3,550.
options.why: Guests liked the boxes, but they had no new reason to order. The boxes cost a lot and brought very few extra buyers. Your K-factor barely changed.
options.better: Give ₹50 off to the family and ₹50 off to each friend who orders. This encourages buyers to bring friends.

screens.text: A growth ___ helps each buyer bring another buyer. So you don't have to ___ to find every new buyer.
screens.why: Exactly. Every Hotmail email carried its message. Your cake boxes carry your cards and your offer to bring friends.

summary: In a growth loop, each buyer helps bring another buyer. People telling friends about you is the oldest kind of loop.
K-factor = new buyers ÷ buyers who brought them. Below 1, you still need other ways to find buyers.
Make it easy for buyers to tell friends. Give them a reason to share. Then count how many new buyers came from them.

cards.front: 30 buyers bring 15 new buyers. What's the K-factor?
cards.back: 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5. Each buyer brings 0.5 new buyers on average.

cards.front: Which builds a loop for a tiffin service?
options: A referral offer for both sides
cards.back: A loop uses something buyers already do to bring new buyers. Ads stop bringing people when you stop paying.

cards.front: Your K-factor is 0.4. Can you stop using all other ways to find buyers?
cards.back: No. Below 1, each group brings fewer new buyers than the last. You still need other ways to find buyers.
